chunks: How multiphase increases output current. The question: How do they increase output current?
Each phase has its own inductor and switches, and all of them feed the same output. The currents add together, so the total is the sum of the phase currents.
No single stage has to carry the full load. This is how a supply can deliver far more current than one inductor and one pair of switches could handle.
Picture four hoses filling one tank. Each hose can only carry so much water, but together they fill the tank four times as fast.
The tank is the output node, the point where all the phases join.
The analogy breaks down in one important way: if the hoses are not evenly open, the one that is most open reaches its limit first, so you cannot count on the full total.
Three phase currents (from the three inductors) merge at the output node. Each carries I out over 3 when balanced.
Phase current: the average current in one phase's inductor. Kirchhoff's current law (KCL): the currents flowing into a junction (node) add up to the current flowing out.
Derated rating: the safe current for a part after allowing for heat. Imbalance: a phase carrying more than its share ("How multiphase bucks work and their challenges").
Saturation current: the current above which an inductor suddenly loses most of its inductance.
A 60 amps load is shared by four phases, so each carries about 15 amps. That is much easier than one stage at 60 amps.
Going the other way, suppose each stage is rated 25 amps after derating. Four stages could carry 100 amps if perfectly balanced.
If mismatch is 5%, the busiest phase hits its limit first, so the usable total is about 4 times 25 over 1. 05 about 95 amps. That is the whole idea.
"The phase inductor currents all feed the same output node, so by KCL they add: four phases at 15 amps each deliver 60 amps.
Each stage only needs FETs, an inductor and a package rated for its own share, so the single-stage limits go away.

In practice the total is N times the derated phase limit divided by one plus the sharing error, and I'd check inductor peak current against saturation and think about what happens if one phase fails."
